value.overview: The Rufous-collared Sparrow (Zonotrichia capensis) is a familiar New World sparrow of open and semi-open habitats from Mexico and the Caribbean south through the Andes and much of southern South America. It often lives near people and is recognized by its gray head, black facial stripes, rusty collar, streaked back, and clear song. In Costa Rica it is a common highland bird, locally called come maíz, meaning “corn eater.”
value.classification: The Rufous-collared Sparrow belongs to the sparrow family Passerellidae and the genus Zonotrichia. Numerous geographic forms are recognized across its broad range; the Costa Rican population is generally associated with the subspecies Zonotrichia capensis costaricensis.
value.identification: This medium-small sparrow has a gray head marked with black stripes through the eye and along the crown, a distinct rusty collar on the nape and sides of the neck, and brown, black-streaked upperparts. The throat is white, while the breast and flanks are pale grayish or buff, often with a dark central breast mark. Two pale wing bars are visible. Juveniles are duller, with less distinct head markings and more heavily streaked underparts.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from southeastern Mexico and Hispaniola through Central and South America to Tierra del Fuego. In Costa Rica it is a regular, locally abundant resident of the highlands, especially from roughly 600 to 3,000 meters elevation. It favors pasture, agricultural land, gardens, roadsides, open woodland, scrub, and urban edges, while generally avoiding unbroken humid forest. It is especially characteristic of the Central Valley and other mountain regions, where it commonly forages on open ground.
value.migrationStatus: In Costa Rica, the Rufous-collared Sparrow is generally resident year-round rather than a long-distance migrant. Individuals may make local movements associated with elevation, rainfall, food availability, or breeding conditions. Elsewhere in the species’ range, particularly in southern South America, some populations undertake seasonal movements.
value.breeding: Breeding can occur during favorable periods, commonly beginning with the rainy season in tropical areas when food becomes more plentiful. The female usually builds a compact cup-shaped nest from grasses and other plant fibers, placing it in low vegetation or near the ground. Clutches generally contain two to five pale greenish-blue eggs marked with brown. Incubation is performed mainly by the female, while both parents feed and care for the nestlings after hatching.
value.dietFeeding: The Rufous-collared Sparrow feeds mainly on seeds, grains, and other plant material, supplemented by insects and other small invertebrates, especially during the breeding season. In Costa Rica it often feeds on lawns, paths, field margins, gardens, and cultivated ground. It usually searches on the ground, walking or hopping while picking up food, and may join mixed-species flocks or take advantage of scattered grain near human settlements.
value.behavior: This active, mostly ground-feeding sparrow is often seen singly, in pairs, or in small groups. It frequently sings from exposed perches such as shrubs, fences, wires, and buildings, and its song varies geographically, producing recognizable regional forms of the species’ vocal pattern. Rufous-collared Sparrows defend breeding territories, but females may have overlapping territories. The species is adaptable and commonly tolerates gardens, farms, parks, and urban neighborhoods.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered stable, with no evidence of a major overall decline.
